claim: Traffic signals adapt through a stigmergy-inspired mechanism where intersections indirectly coordinate through environmental modifications (traffic flow patterns) rather than direct communication.
mechanism: Each intersection adjusts its signal timing based on local traffic conditions and the residual effects of previous timing decisions (traffic platoons, queue formations). These effects create an 'environmental' pattern that influences neighboring intersections without explicit communication. The system exhibits emergent coordination through these indirect feedback loops.
evidence: Stigmergy has been observed in biological systems to achieve complex coordination
Traffic platoons naturally form and influence downstream intersections
Emergent behavior has been observed in some traffic signal systems
assumptions: Traffic patterns created by one intersection serve as sufficient information for neighbors
Indirect coordination can achieve near-optimal performance
The system can distinguish between beneficial and detrimental environmental patterns
expected_failure_modes: Propagation of timing errors through the network
Inability to adapt to network-wide disruptions
Suboptimal coordination due to limited environmental information
novelty_rationale: Applies the biological principle of stigmergy to traffic signal control, eliminating the need for explicit communication between intersections while still achieving coordination.
testability: Can be tested by implementing a system where intersections only respond to local traffic conditions without direct communication and measuring emergent coordination and system performance.
falsifier: If the system fails to achieve coordination between non-adjacent intersections or produces significantly worse performance than centrally optimized signals, this hypothesis would be proven wrong.
